Am I required to buy it?

Federal law requires it only in a high-risk zone (A or V) with a federally regulated or backed mortgage, or federal help to buy or build (42 U.S.C. §4012a). Outside those zones, a lender may still require it.

81.4% of Kentucky's NFIP policy units are in high-risk zones (not 81.4% of all buildings, and not an answer about your own home).

Of the NFIP claim dollars paid here (1978–2026), 19.7% went to claims rated outside high-risk zones A and V. That uses the zone on each claim, not today's map, and leaves out claims with no zone.

Flood zonePolicy unitsShare
Zone AE (high-risk)10,69661.3%
Zone A (high-risk)3,48320.0%
Zone X3,20918.4%
Other high-risk zones (AH, A06, A07, A03 and others)270.2%
Other low-risk or unclassified zones330.2%

Policy records keep the code they were rated with, so older labels such as A1 to A30 are counted on their own. Every zone starting with A or V is high-risk; A1 to A30 and AE are the same kind of area (44 CFR §64.3).

Insured units by the zone each policy is rated in. How this is counted What each means: zone AE, zone X, zone VE. Find yours with the flood zone map lookup by address.

Not in the NFIP (58 communities here): Bedford; Bellefonte; Blaine; Burnside; Campbellsburg; Campton; Carrsville; Casey County (unincorporated area only); Clarkson, Cityof; Concord; Corinth; Crittenden; Cumberland County (unincorporated area only); Dixon; Drakesboro; Dry Ridge; Eddyville; Elsmere; Eminence; Fairview; Ferguson; Fordsville; Fort Mitchell; Fountain Run; Fox Chase; Gamaliel; Grand Rivers; Hebron Estates; Hickman County (unincorporated area only); Kuttawa; La Center; La Grange; Lafayette; Lakeside Park; Loretto; Mackville; Mchenry; North Middletown; Owingsville; Park City; Pembroke; Pewee Valley; Pippa Passes; Powderly; Raywick; River Bluff; Rockport; Russell Springs; Salem; Sandy Hook; Smithfield; Sonora; South Carrollton; Whitesville; Williamstown; Willisburg; Wolfe County (unincorporated area only); Woodbury. Federal flood insurance (NFIP) is sold only in communities that take part in the NFIP; in a community that has not joined, or once a suspension takes effect, no one can buy an NFIP policy.

Flood insurance cost in Kentucky

In Kentucky, typically about $1,195 a year ($100 a month), fees included. Half of homeowners here pay between $837 and $1,736. To check a quote, use the checker at the top.

A quarter pay under $837 · Typical $1,195 · A quarter pay over $1,736 · A tenth pay $2,648 or more

Each policy's annual cost (premium plus the federal policy fee, reserve fund assessment and HFIAA surcharge), single-family primary residences. The bar is the middle half of policies, from 9,882 single-family primary-home policies. These are existing policies, many still below FEMA's full-risk price.

The NFIP also offers policies for renters and businesses. The median here is for single-family primary-home policies, not businesses or second homes. Renting? See what renters pay.

Source: floodsmart.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

How do I actually get covered — and how fast?

Most policies start 30 days after you buy. Bought while making, increasing, extending or renewing a mortgage, it can start at closing if the insurer is paid within 10 days (30 if the lender, title company or settlement attorney pays).

  • Waiting period30 days
  • Bought with a new or refinanced mortgageCan start at closing, if paid in time
  • NFIP building limit$250,000
  • NFIP contents limit$100,000

Most homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage. Does homeowners insurance cover flooding? To buy: call the NFIP at (877) 336-2627, go to FloodSmart.gov, or ask any licensed insurance agent. Every NFIP insurer offers the same rates.

Already flooded? Insured: report the loss to your insurance agent or company now (FEMA's steps: how to start a flood claim), and send a proof of loss (your signed, sworn statement of the amount you are claiming) within 60 days of the flood (44 CFR 61, App. A(1), Art. VII). Not insured: a policy bought today will not cover a flood that already happened, and FEMA disaster aid is open to people in counties designated in a federally declared disaster.

Wait exceptions, exclusions, premium increases and surcharges, aid, appeals, rebuilding and closing rules: the NFIP rules in full.

Your state's insurance regulator: Kentucky Department of Insurance.

Source: floodsmart.gov, agents.floodsmart.gov, fema.gov, ecfr.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

Flood insurance claims in Kentucky: what floods pay out

Floods in Kentucky have led to 27,308 NFIP flood claims and $524.2 million in payouts since 1978; the worst years were 2025, 1997 and 2010.

Bar height is dollars paid that year. Orange bars are the three costliest years: 2025 ($112,418,827), 1997 ($79,683,887), 2010 ($38,003,383). Total paid $524,157,483. Totals for 2025 and 2026 are not final while their claims stay open. How this is counted

Do flood claims here actually pay out?

Most do: 86.5% of claims in Kentucky paid something. The average paid claim was $22,330 (all years, in dollars of the day, not adjusted for inflation).

Typical claim: the median paid building claim was $8,371.

  • Average paid claim, incl. code-upgrade (ICC) pay$22,330
  • No recorded payment13.5%
  • Claims that paid23,612

FEMA's claim records give a reason when a building claim has no recorded payment, such as damage less than the deductible, not an actual flood, seepage or backed-up drains. The average is over claims that paid something and includes Increased Cost of Compliance payments (help to elevate or rebuild to code), which the yearly totals above leave out. Dollars are as paid at the time, not adjusted for inflation; a single home can file across several floods over the years. All years, records FEMA coded as entered in error left out (the claims page uses losses from 2020 on, so its shares differ). FEMA's data has no open or closed field, so a recent claim with no payment may still be paid.

Would a policy here pay to rebuild my home?

Not in full for at least 14.0% of the 6,372 single-family policies here that report a rebuilding cost: FEMA's records put it above the NFIP's $250,000 building limit.

  • Rebuilding cost above the building limit (of 6,372 policies reporting one)14.0%
  • Single-family policies insured to the building maximum (all of them, not only those above)26.6%
  • Damage was more than the coverage (of 22,281 claims paid with a damage figure)8.7%

The two shares have different bases: insured-to-the-maximum counts every single-family policy with the full building limit; the rebuilding-cost share counts only the policies that report a rebuilding cost. Homes insured for less than their own rebuilding cost can also fall short. How this is counted

The NFIP pays the cost to rebuild (not a depreciated value) only for a single-family home that is your principal residence and is insured for at least 80% of its full rebuilding cost, or for the $250,000 maximum.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies; FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data effective August 31, 2026; retrieved November 13, 2026.

What does it cost in my flood zone?

From about $990 a year (Zone X) to $1,424 (Zone A) here. Your zone is on your lender's flood determination or FEMA's map; find its row below.

Flood zoneMedian / yrPriced policies
Zone AE$1,2396,533
Zone X$9901,988
Zone A$1,4241,345

What the zone codes mean (44 CFR §64.3): A, AE and A1–A30 are high-risk; AO and AH are high-risk with shallow flooding; A99 is high-risk behind a flood barrier FEMA treats as complete; V, VE and V1–V30 are coastal high-risk, flooded by tides with fast-moving water (velocity); B and X are areas of moderate flood hazard, C and X areas of minimal hazard; D has possible but undetermined flood hazards. A 1 percent or greater chance a year works out to a 26% or greater chance of at least one such flood over 30 years.

Zones with fewer than 50 priced single-family policies are omitted. Your own premium still depends on elevation and coverage.

Source: ecfr.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

Why do sites quote different prices for Kentucky?

Because they measure different things. Existing single-family policies here typically cost $1,195 a year, and policies first bought in the past year $1,206; other sites count other policies, years or averages.

MeasureAmountWhat it counts
Typical cost, single-family homes (median)$1,195premium plus fees; the middle policy
Typical premium only$952before the federal fee, reserve fund and surcharge
Typical cost, policies whose term began Jan–Aug 2026$1,2306,660 policies
Typical cost, policies first bought in the past year$1,206838 policies, past year
FEMA's full-risk premium (median)$1,388the price FEMA's model sets for these existing policies
Full-risk premium plus average fees$1,671what these existing policies would cost at FEMA's full price
Average (mean) cost, single-family homes$1,452pulled up by a few expensive policies
Average cost, every policy type$1,923adds condos, rentals and businesses

Condo owners: condo-unit policies are 1.0% of NFIP policy units here and whole condo buildings 7.6%. The every-policy-type average includes them. Condo-unit policies here have a median cost of $643 a year (premium plus fees, 171 priced policies; condo flood insurance by state). The single-family figures leave out every policy FEMA marks as a condo unit or a whole condo building.

All from the NFIP policies in force on August 31, 2026. How this is counted

How do current premiums compare with FEMA's full-risk price?

51.4% of single-family primary-home policies in Kentucky have a premium below FEMA's full-risk premium, so those policies' bills are rising toward it. Median premium $952, full-risk $1,388 (premiums only, before fees).

  • Median premium charged (before fees)$952
  • Median full-risk premium$1,388
  • Pay below full-risk51.4% of 9,882

Yearly cap: By law, most premium rates may not rise more than 18% a year (42 U.S.C. §4015(e)).

Source: agents.floodsmart.gov, govinfo.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

How Kentucky appears in the national research papers

Each paper measures one thing in FEMA's records for every U.S. county with enough records. A fifth is a position in a list, not a grade or a prediction.

  • Flood damage over building coverage: NFIP claims by county: 6 of this state's counties have at least 100 paid single-family primary-home claims with recorded damage and coverage and are listed.
  • Outside the zone: paid flood claims rated outside high-risk zones: 12 of this state's counties have at least 100 claims with a payment and a rated zone and are listed.

Can I pay less?

The usual building deductible here is $2,000 (37.2% of single-family policies). FEMA's ways that may lower an NFIP bill: a higher deductible (you pay more of any loss), work that lowers the building's flood risk, and an Elevation Certificate.

Do the same homes flood again here?

Yes: FEMA's disaster-aid records hold 11,392 damage records from homes here that flooded more than once; 805 records are from homes FEMA's disaster-aid data flags as severe repeat-loss (SRL).

  • Repeat-flood damage records11,392
  • Records from homes flagged severe repeat-loss (SRL)805

These count damage events on repeat-flooded homes, not distinct homes. How this is counted

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Individual Assistance Multiple-Loss Flood Properties. Data: FEMA's current multiple-loss list; retrieved November 13, 2026.

How often is Kentucky a flood disaster?

63 federal disasters for floods or storms here; the latest was Severe Storms, Straight-Line Winds, Flooding, Landslides, and Mudslides (2026).

  • September 2026 — Severe Storms, Straight-Line Winds, Flooding, Landslides, and Mudslides
  • April 2025 — Severe Storms, Straight-Line Winds, Tornadoes, Flooding, Landslides, and Mudslides
  • April 2025 — Severe Storms, Straight-Line Winds, Tornadoes, and Flooding (emergency declaration)
  • February 2025 — Severe Storms, Straight-Line Winds, Flooding, Landslides, and Mudslides
  • February 2025 — Severe Storms, Straight-Line Winds, Flooding, and Landslides (emergency declaration)
  • November 2024 — Remnants of Hurricane Helene

Only the latest are listed, newest first; disasters with the same month and title share one line, which says how many; the count covers every flood, hurricane, tropical-storm and coastal-storm declaration FEMA lists here, plus severe-storm declarations whose title names flooding, including emergency declarations. How this is counted

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Disaster Declarations Summaries. Data: declarations through 2026; retrieved November 13, 2026.

Did FEMA aid homeowners after floods and storms?

Yes: FEMA approved $338.3 million for homeowners here after floods and storms, about $4,543 per registration.

FEMA disaster aid helps with uninsured and underinsured losses, and is separate from NFIP insurance. The average is over every registration, including those approved for nothing. Only disasters counted in the flood-disaster card are included; their aid can still cover wind or tornado damage from the same storm. Disasters for COVID, fire, winter storms or tornadoes alone are left out.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Housing Assistance (Owners). Data: homeowner aid by disaster; retrieved November 13, 2026.

Are these counts complete?

Every record FEMA's download lists was received and counted.

In-force count: 17,448 policy units (from 16,678 API records; condo-association records carry more than one unit).
